title: The bad student answers
sentences: THE BAD STUDENT ANSWERS
No, he couldn't possibly have guessed it would come today, really.
Well, he had been expecting it, of course he had, and he'd even dreamed something of the sort last night:
but in his dream he was called up in Hungarian, true, and it seemed as though Mr. Fröhlich taught Hungarian too.
In his dream he disposed of the whole question, answered about parallel lines, and got an Alpha Minus.
When his name is called, he cannot believe his ears; he looks round: perhaps a miracle will happen, perhaps it is only a hallucination,
a crushing nightmare that this is his name, and that he will now wake from this dream.
Then he scoops up a pile of exercise-books from his desk.
While he walks down the little aisle between the rows of desks, he thinks: "Ay plus bee by ay minus bee equals ay square minus bee square."
That is what he will be asked.
He is sure that is what he will be asked.
"If he asks anything else, I'll transfer with a supplementary exam to the civilian school and take up a military career."
Meanwhile he stumbles and drops his exercise-books.
While he picks them up from the floor, the obligatory laughter rings out behind his back,
which this time nobody forbids: the bad student stands outside the law; one may laugh at him.
The teacher sits down and places the notebook before him.
He looks up.
The bad student convulsively keeps repeating to himself: "ay plus bee..."
He takes the chalk.
The teacher looks at him.
- Are you prepared?
- says the teacher.
- I am prepared.
Oh yes, of course he is prepared.
Even the condemned man prepares himself: he receives the last rites and has his hair cut off.
- Well then, write it.
The bad student turns toward the blackboard.
- bee square minus plus minus square root bee minus four ay cee by two ay.
And the bad student obediently begins to write and repeats the figures after them.
He writes and writes, like Mrs Ágnes; he knows what it is about; he sees the problem "just as
as that night," when he fell asleep beside it without the faintest idea of what the whole thing meant.
Yes, this is it; he dimly suspects it is some quadratic equation - but what will come of it.
He writes slowly and calligraphically.
He thickens the stem of the four - from the line that means a fraction he carefully rubs off a bit; for this he makes a special trip to the window for the sponge.
He gains time with this.
Perhaps the bell will ring in the meantime.
Or something will happen.
He will not be on the platform long anyway.
He still writes this down, and puts up the equals sign slowly too - yes,
he still does this like other, higher beings, like a good student.
He still writes up "a 2".
In the military school you have to get up very early; the thought flashes through his mind, suddenly.
But then one becomes a lieutenant.
Perhaps one gets posted to Fiume.
Meanwhile he writes slowly - he still has not finished writing it.
An outsider watching this scene would think some good student was answering.
But the expert already knows what it means when someone draws the tail of a two with such boundless care.
Deadly silence all around.
The teacher does not stir.
Now he must speak.
- The quadratic equation...
- he begins intelligently, with narrowed eyes, and watches the blackboard with deep attention.
- The quadratic equation...
- he repeats in the manner of one who does not repeat the word as though he did not know what he wanted to say,
but rather because from his vast store of things to say he selects and weighs the most correct, the most striking, the most perfect.
But the teacher - oh, the teacher already knows what this means.
- Are you prepared?
- he says harshly and dryly.
- Please, sir, I am prepared.
Murderous defiance and rebellious despair tremble in his voice.
- Well then, let us hear it.
The bad student takes a deep breath.
- The quadratic equation is derived from the linear equation in such a way that we multiply the whole equation...
And now he is speaking.
He is saying something.
At the second sentence he expected to be interrupted - he steals a glance at the teacher.
But he stares with an unmoving face, saying neither that it is good nor that it is bad.
He does not speak.
Yet the bad student knows very well that what he is saying cannot be right.
Then why does the teacher not speak?
This is terrible.
His voice begins to tremble.
Suddenly he sees the teacher lift the notebook.
At this he turns pale and begins at a dizzying speed:
- The quadratic equation is derived from the first in such a way that through...
Please, sir, I am prepared.
- Ernő Polgár - says the teacher loudly.
What is this?
Have they already called up someone else?
Are they finished with him?
What is this?
Is he dreaming?
- The quadratic equation...
- he begins again, menacingly.
Ernő Polgár comes out briskly, and at the other end of the blackboard he is already taking the other piece of chalk.
- The quadratic...
Please, sir, I am prepared.
Nobody answers.
And now he stands there, alone in the crowd, like on an island.
But he does not go back to his seat yet.
Nobody told him to go back to his seat - hollow and shabby, with an outcast heart he stands there - nobody told him, nobody told him.
He is still answering.
Should he now walk back again between the rows of desks?
No, he prefers to stand there, foolishly: his hand fumbles stammeringly on the blackboard, among the wreckage of the half-finished equation,
like a crashed pilot over the burst cylinders of his engine.
Meanwhile the other boy is already answering too.
He is talking about parallel lines - that too is as strange and odd...
as everything...
they have been busy with around him here for years...
busy cheerfully and springily and loudly...
and of which he never understood anything...
he has memorized a few sentences so far, and floated on those...
And so he stands now, still standing, hoping, politely listening to what the other is saying...
now and then he nods approvingly, at least to show that he prepared, that he knows...
sometimes he even speaks up timidly, rocking himself in the illusion that he was the one questioned, but only softly, so they will not send him back to his seat...
then modestly he falls silent and listens...
he leans forward, takes part in the recitation, hands over the chalk, bustles around the one answering, even prompts him,
loudly, not in order to help, but so the teacher will see that he prompts, therefore he knows...
In a word: he does not give up.
Then once his strength leaves him; he falls silent, and once again he thinks of the military school.
In his darkening mind, like distant words, the noises echo back...
the crackling of chalk...
the faces flow away, and for a moment he clearly sees the infinite,
about which the one answering has just declared that there parallel lines meet.
He sees the infinite...
big, blue something...
to one side there is also a little house, with written above: "Entrance to the fourth infinite."
In the house there are coat-racks where the parallel lines hang up their hats, then go through into the room, sit down in the desk, and greet one another joyfully...
the parallel lines, yes...
in the class of the infinite, of understanding, of goodness and brotherly love, which he will never reach...
that "upper form" into which he may "never be promoted owing to unsatisfactory results."
